{{Short description|Concept in mathematical set theory}}
{{No footnotes|date=January 2020}}

In [[mathematics]], particularly in [[set theory]], '''Fodor's lemma''' (or the '''pressing-down lemma''') states:
{{Math theorem
| name = Fodor's lemma
| math_statement =If <math>\kappa</math> is a [[Regular cardinal|regular]], [[uncountable]] [[Cardinal number|cardinal]], <math>S</math> is a [[stationary set|stationary subset]] of <math>\kappa</math>, and <math>f:S\rightarrow\kappa</math> is regressive (that is, <math>f(\alpha)<\alpha</math> for any <math>\alpha\in S</math>, <math>\alpha\neq 0</math>) then there is some <math>\gamma</math> and some stationary <math>S_0\subseteq S</math> such that <math>f(\alpha)=\gamma</math> for any <math>\alpha\in S_0</math>.
}}

In modern parlance, the nonstationary ideal is ''normal''. The lemma was first proved by the Hungarian set theorist, [[Géza Fodor (mathematician)|Géza Fodor]] in 1956.

{{Math proof
| title=Proof
| proof=
We can assume that <math>0\notin S</math> (by removing 0, if necessary).
If Fodor's lemma is false, for every <math>\alpha<\kappa</math> there is some [[club set]] <math>C_\alpha</math> such that <math>C_\alpha\cap f^{-1}(\alpha)=\emptyset</math>. Let <math>C=\Delta_{\alpha<\kappa} C_\alpha</math>. The club sets are closed under [[diagonal intersection]], so <math>C</math> is also club and therefore there is some <math>\alpha\in S\cap C</math>. Then <math>\alpha\in C_\beta</math> for each <math>\beta<\alpha</math>, and so there can be no <math>\beta<\alpha</math> such that <math>\alpha\in f^{-1}(\beta)</math>, so <math>f(\alpha)\geq\alpha</math>, a [[contradiction]].
}}There is a Fodor's lemma for trees:{{Math theorem
| name = Fodor's lemma for trees
| math_statement = For every non-special [[Tree (set theory)|tree]] <math>T</math> and regressive mapping <math>f:T\rightarrow T</math> (that is, <math>f(t)<t</math>, with respect to the order on <math>T</math>, for every <math>t\in T</math>, <math>t\neq 0</math>), there is a non-special subtree <math>S\subseteq T</math> on which <math>f</math> is constant.
}}
Fodor's lemma also holds for [[Thomas Jech]]'s notion of stationary sets as well as for the [[Stationary set#Generalized notion|general notion]] of stationary set.
